trends.title: Intergenerational fiscal rebalancing
trends.narrative: OECD governments are redistributing fiscal burdens between generations through tax, pension, housing and benefit reform — Australia legislating, UK commissioning, Canada debating spending-side reform.

no_change.headline: Deferral continues
no_change.text: Pension, housing and debt burdens keep shifting quietly onto younger and future taxpayers. Reform is announced and diluted; the political cost of confronting older voter blocs keeps the status quo in place.

marginal.headline: Trimming at the edges
marginal.text: Retirement ages nudge up, some inheritance and property reliefs narrow, and youth guarantees expand modestly. The direction of travel is fairer but the pace is slow and easily reversed by an electoral cycle.

adaptive.headline: Structural rebalancing
adaptive.text: Several OECD states pair pension reform with serious housing and tax-base changes, framed explicitly as generational fairness. A durable cross-party settlement emerges in at least one country and becomes a reference model.

radical.headline: Wealth-transfer reset
radical.text: Inheritance, property and wealth taxation move to the centre of fiscal policy, redistributing accumulated advantage toward younger cohorts. Housing is treated as an intergenerational-justice question, not only an affordability one.

leading_indicators.text: A G7 government passes pension and housing reform under one fairness banner
Organised older-voter mobilisation forces a reform reversal
A major economy enacts a standing wealth or inheritance tax rise framed generationally

trends.title: Youth climate litigation: international advance, domestic retreat
trends.narrative: International law is opening to youth climate claims (ICJ, UNGA, Bonaire) while US federal courts systematically close (Lighthiser, Genesis B., Wisconsin) — pushing strategy toward state courts and treaty mechanisms.

no_change.headline: Two-track stalemate
no_change.text: International law keeps recognising climate duties while domestic courts, especially in the US, keep closing the door on youth standing. The gap between advisory principle and enforceable remedy stays wide.

marginal.headline: Selective openings
marginal.text: A few state or national courts accept narrow youth climate claims, and the ICJ opinion is cited more often. Wins stay jurisdiction-specific and are met with legislative pushback elsewhere.

adaptive.headline: Doctrine travels
adaptive.text: ICJ-derived duties begin entering domestic merits rulings, and a line of favourable youth cases hardens into citable doctrine. Litigation risk starts shaping government and corporate climate conduct.

radical.headline: Enforceable duty of care
radical.text: Courts across multiple jurisdictions recognise an enforceable climate duty owed to the young and unborn, backed by remedies. Litigation becomes a reliable lever, and climate inaction carries hard legal cost.

leading_indicators.text: A domestic merits ruling relies on the ICJ advisory opinion
Several jurisdictions recognise an enforceable climate duty to future generations
A supreme court forecloses youth standing and others follow

trends.title: Future generations institutional machinery
trends.narrative: Dedicated institutions for representing future generations are multiplying: EU strategy and index, Welsh commissioner model, UNU platform, generational impact assessment laws, and SRM governance debates about the truly unborn.

no_change.headline: Isolated experiments
no_change.text: Future-generations commissioners and councils remain scattered pilots, admired but rarely copied, and vulnerable to defunding. The UN-level ambition stays aspirational without machinery underneath it.

marginal.headline: Slow replication
marginal.text: The Welsh-style model is adopted by a few more jurisdictions and referenced in UN processes. Mandates vary widely and durability is untested through hostile governments.

adaptive.headline: A standardising network
adaptive.text: A transnational peer network forms among future-generations institutions, converging mandates and giving the model institutional durability. The UN Declaration acquires implementing bodies rather than only text.

radical.headline: Guardians with teeth
radical.text: Future-generations institutions gain investigatory power, statutory triggers and standing to challenge decisions. Representing the unborn becomes an enforceable function of the state, not an advisory courtesy.

leading_indicators.text: Future-generations institutions form a standing international network
A commissioner gains statutory power to block or delay a decision
An established commissioner is abolished after a change of government

trends.title: Youth digital protection regulatory wave
trends.narrative: One of the fastest-spreading regulatory trends in digital governance: under-16 social media bans across four countries in six months, G7 common principles, EU age verification — countered by OHCHR's safety-by-design framework.

no_change.headline: Bans without design
no_change.text: Under-16 restrictions and age checks spread as headline measures, but the underlying platform design that drives harm is untouched. Enforcement is thin and workarounds are trivial, so protection is more announced than felt.

marginal.headline: Patchwork tightening
marginal.text: More countries add age verification and duty-of-care rules, and platforms make selective adjustments. Standards diverge across borders, creating compliance friction without yet forcing a shared safety-by-design baseline.

adaptive.headline: Safety by design
adaptive.text: Regulators converge on design-level obligations — default protections, auditable risk duties, independent oversight — rather than blunt bans. Platforms rebuild youth experiences around these duties and cross-border alignment firms up.

radical.headline: Structural liability
radical.text: Binding, enforceable duties with real penalties make platforms liable for foreseeable youth harm. Business models change because the cost of harmful design finally lands on the designer, not the child.

leading_indicators.text: A major bloc adopts enforceable safety-by-design duties over blanket bans
A regulator wins a penalty case establishing platform liability for youth harm
Flagship bans prove unenforceable and quietly lapse

trends.title: AI global governance architecture is institutionalising
trends.narrative: From Global Digital Compact Objective 5 and the UN AI scientific panel/dialogue track through EU AI Act implementation, national safety institutes, and Council of Europe rights instruments — AI governance is shifting from principles to permanent machinery, with youth and child-safety rules running in parallel.

no_change.headline: Fragmented guardrails
no_change.text: National rules, voluntary commitments and multilateral principles continue to multiply without interoperable enforcement. Youth and future-generations concerns appear in language but rarely shape model deployment, procurement or remedy.

marginal.headline: Standards begin to align
marginal.text: Major jurisdictions converge on shared risk vocabulary, incident reporting and child-safety expectations. Compliance remains uneven, but regulators and standards bodies reduce the most costly gaps between regimes.

adaptive.headline: Interoperable accountability
adaptive.text: Cross-border assurance, independent evaluation and rights-based impact duties become mutually recognised. Public institutions can compare model risks and enforce remedies while youth participation becomes a recurring part of governance design.

radical.headline: Global duties with remedy
radical.text: A binding international framework establishes enforceable duties for frontier AI, public-interest access to evidence, and remedies for affected communities. Long-term and intergenerational impacts become explicit tests for deployment.

leading_indicators.text: Two major AI regimes recognise each other's independent assurance results
A multilateral agreement creates binding incident disclosure and remedy duties
Competing national standards harden into incompatible compliance blocs

trends.title: Youth participation in governance institutions
trends.narrative: Youth voice is being institutionalized across multilateral and national governance — UN forums, EU dialogues, national youth councils — while exclusion persists (Zimbabwe, India) and youth political power erupts outside institutions (Nepal).

no_change.headline: Consultation theatre
no_change.text: Youth councils and advisory bodies keep multiplying, but real decision power stays elsewhere. Participation is symbolic, episodic and easily ignored when it is inconvenient to those who hold the budget and the vote.

marginal.headline: Seats at more tables
marginal.text: Youth delegates gain formal presence in more forums and occasional voting rights. Influence remains uneven and personality-dependent, but the expectation that young people are consulted becomes harder to skip openly.

adaptive.headline: Binding youth checks
adaptive.text: Some jurisdictions give youth bodies statutory footing — mandatory consultation, published responses, and youth-impact tests with real procedural teeth. Tokenism becomes politically costly and participation starts to bite on outcomes.

radical.headline: Shared decision power
radical.text: Lowered voting ages, co-decision mandates and enforceable youth-representation quotas move young people from advised to deciding. Institutions redesign around durable youth authority rather than time-limited pilots.

leading_indicators.text: A national parliament makes youth-impact consultation legally binding
A country lowers its voting age with cross-party support
Flagship youth councils lapse after their founding champions leave office

trends.title: Intergenerational equity goes mainstream
trends.narrative: Intergenerational equity language is migrating from advocacy into budgets, court citations, mass media and domains far beyond climate — disability policy, national security, space governance, fiscal federalism.

no_change.headline: Rhetoric without teeth
no_change.text: Intergenerational-fairness language stays a framing device in speeches and strategy documents, but budgets, mandates and laws are unchanged. The vocabulary spreads while the distribution of resources between generations holds where it is.

marginal.headline: Soft duties appear
marginal.text: A handful of governments attach non-binding future-generations tests to budgets and impact assessments. Compliance is patchy and reversible, but a shared methodology begins to form and early adopters cite each other.

adaptive.headline: Institutionalised checks
adaptive.text: Future-generations commissioners, statutory well-being duties and generational impact assessments become standard machinery in several OECD states, surviving changes of government and reshaping how major fiscal and environmental decisions are justified.

radical.headline: Constitutional standing
radical.text: Intergenerational equity acquires enforceable status — constitutional clauses, binding duties and courts willing to strike down decisions that offload cost onto the unborn. The principle reorders budgeting rather than annotating it.

leading_indicators.text: A second national government legislates a binding generational-impact test on budgets
A high court voids a policy citing intergenerational-equity duties
Commissioners created in one term are quietly defunded in the next

trends.title: Youth climate & environment governance
trends.narrative: Structured pipelines from youth climate organizing into formal governance: national youth climate councils, COP31 talanoa dialogues, EU green policy dialogues, and long-term environment planning frameworks.

no_change.headline: Voice without leverage
no_change.text: Youth climate delegations attend, speak and are thanked, while the decisions that matter are taken without binding regard to their input. Access grows but leverage over outcomes does not.

marginal.headline: Formalised inclusion
marginal.text: Youth constituencies gain more standing places in climate processes and occasional negotiating roles. Their fingerprints appear on some texts, though the core bargaining still happens among states and blocs.

adaptive.headline: Governed-in youth
adaptive.text: Youth roles become embedded features of climate governance — funded delegations, guaranteed submissions, accountability mechanisms — that persist across summits rather than being renegotiated each year.

radical.headline: Rights-anchored authority
radical.text: Youth climate participation fuses with rights-based obligations, giving young people enforceable standing to shape and challenge climate decisions. Participation becomes a duty owed to them, not a courtesy extended.

leading_indicators.text: A climate process guarantees funded youth delegations and published responses
A rights ruling gives youth enforceable standing in climate decisions
Youth roles shrink back to side events after a flagship summit

trends.title: Education equity & intergenerational mobility
trends.narrative: Discovered cluster around education, unesco — confirmed from 11 signals spanning 5 existing trend(s).

no_change.headline: Framework on a shelf
no_change.text: Futures-education and UNESCO framing circulates in conferences and guidance but does not reach curricula or classrooms at scale. It stays a specialist vocabulary rather than a change in what students learn.

marginal.headline: Pilot uptake
marginal.text: A cluster of ministries and networks pilot futures literacy and anticipatory education. Adoption is enthusiast-driven and uneven, but early evidence and shared materials begin to accumulate.

adaptive.headline: Into the curriculum
adaptive.text: Futures thinking is written into national curricula and teacher training in several systems, backed by assessment and funding, moving from pilot to standard practice in those jurisdictions.

radical.headline: Anticipatory schooling
radical.text: Anticipation and long-term thinking become organising principles of mainstream education, reshaping curricula, pedagogy and how systems judge success — a structural shift in what schooling is for.

leading_indicators.text: A national curriculum embeds futures literacy with assessment and funding
Multiple systems restructure curricula around anticipatory learning
Pilots end without institutionalisation when grants expire

event_trends.title: Under-16 social media age-gates
event_trends.narrative: Australia enforced an under-16 social-media minimum-age obligation in December 2025. France, Denmark, Greece, Malaysia, Norway, Spain, Indonesia, Poland, the UK, Singapore, Brazil, the Netherlands and others have since enacted, drafted, or committed to similar age-gates. This is a spreading regulatory event class, not the entire youth-digital-protection watch domain.
event_trends.claim: Jurisdictions are adopting minimum-age restrictions on social media for children, clustering around 15–16, from late 2024 through 2026.
